track.name: market-research
track.label: Market Research
track.summary: Learn to design and run primary and secondary research studies, analyse qualitative and quantitative data, and turn findings into clear, actionable recommendations for stakeholders.

phases.title: Fundamentals
phases.description: Understand what market research is, the difference between primary and secondary research, and when to use each approach.

phases.title: Qualitative Methods
phases.description: Master in-depth interviews, focus groups, and ethnographic research — then learn to code and analyse transcripts systematically.

phases.title: Quantitative Methods
phases.description: Design surveys with sound scales and sampling strategies, run A/B tests, and apply conjoint analysis to measure trade-off preferences.

phases.title: Secondary Research & Data Sources
phases.description: Navigate desk research, industry reports, competitive intelligence, and free public data sources effectively.

phases.title: Consumer Insights & Segmentation
phases.description: Build research-backed personas, apply psychographic and behavioural segmentation models, and use the Jobs-to-Be-Done framework.

phases.title: Synthesis & Presentation
phases.description: Turn raw findings into clear recommendations, write compelling executive summaries, and communicate research to stakeholders.

steps.d: Write one clear question you need answered to make a business decision (e.g., 'Will small businesses adopt this workflow?' or 'How much would customers pay?').
Name who needs the research (product, marketing, sales, leadership) and what they'll do differently based on your findings.
Break your research question into 2-3 specific, answerable sub-questions (Who are the customers? What do they value? How do they decide?).
Does this need to be answered before you ship, or can it inform version 2.0? This determines how much research is worth doing.
Outline a simple plan: what you'll do (interview, survey, test), how many people, timeline, and how findings will inform decisions.
Explain primary research: asking people directly (interviews, surveys, tests, observations) to get firsthand answers to your question.
Explain secondary research: using existing data (reports, industry analysis, competitor websites, reviews) to answer your question.
For your business, name 10 sources of existing data: industry reports, competitor reviews, news archives, surveys you can buy, community discussions.
Before doing primary research, do desk research: What's already known about your question? What gaps remain? Who's already studied this?
Plan a research project using both primary (interview 20 customers) and secondary (read 5 industry reports) to triangulate findings.
For your research question, name the deadline (product launch, funding decision) and how quickly an answer is needed.
For interviews (deep, slow, small sample) vs. surveys (broad, fast, risky) vs. testing (costly, realistic, biased by execution), pick the best fit.
For three different research questions (What's the market size? Why do people churn? Do they like our tagline?), recommend a method and explain why.
Before committing to a large study, run a small version (interview 5 people, survey 50, test with 20) to validate your approach.
Write why you chose interview, survey, or testing for your specific question, timeline, and constraints; name the tradeoffs you're making.
For 5-10 open-ended questions, cover: their current approach, pain points, how they decide, budget, and what would change their behavior.
Identify 20-30 people who match your target customer and invite them to 30-minute interviews (offer a small incentive if your budget allows).
Ask your prepared questions, listen more than you talk, probe on surprising answers, and take notes on what they actually do (not just what they say).
After 8-10 interviews, list recurring themes: needs, objections, vocabularies, decision-makers, and alternatives people consider.
Summarize: who your target customer really is, what they actually need, how they currently solve it, and what would motivate a switch.
Recruit 8-12 people who match your target profile, ensure diversity of experience/opinion, and schedule a 90-minute guided discussion.
Plan 6-8 open-ended questions covering their current situation, perceptions, reactions to your idea, and how they'd use it.
Create psychological safety (no judgment), encourage participation from quiet voices, probe on disagreements, and capture both consensus and outliers.
In ethnographic research, watch how customers actually work without prompting; document the workarounds, frustrations, and moments of delight.
Review recordings and notes; document agreed-on needs, conflicting opinions, and mental models that would matter for your product.
Print or digitally display all interview transcripts or notes and do a first pass: what stands out? What's surprising? What's confusing?
Identify recurring themes and create codes (customer need, pain point, objection, decision factor); then mark every mention in your data.
Tally how many times each theme appears; note whether it's mentioned by most respondents (strong pattern) or outliers (interesting edge case).
Group codes into themes: Do certain pain points cluster together? Do specific segments have different needs? What's the hierarchy?
Document your 4-6 main themes with evidence: quotes from respondents, frequency, and what each theme means for your business.
Name 3-5 specific beliefs about customers that matter to your success (e.g., 'They'll adopt mobile-first', 'Price sensitivity is high above $500').
Draft 15-20 clear, unbiased questions using rating scales (1-5 agreement), ranking, multiple choice, and open-ended follow-ups.
Test your survey with 5-10 people: do they understand the questions? Do the answers vary or is everyone saying yes? Refine it.
Use your customer database, social media, or a survey tool to recruit 200-500 people matching your target; incentivize completion.
Look at distributions (what % agree strongly), breakdowns by segment (do SMBs answer differently?), and correlations (Do high-price customers value X more?).
Name the total group you're studying (all SaaS companies, women aged 25-40, US online shoppers) and estimate its size.
Determine how many respondents you need to be confident in findings (use a sample calculator; typically 100-400 for business research).
Random sampling works best but isn't always possible; convenience sampling (easy to reach) is biased but common; document your method.
For your sample size and population, research what margin of error and confidence level you achieve (e.g., ±5% at 95% confidence).
When you report results, state clearly: sample size, how you recruited, response rate, any demographic imbalances, and what you can and can't claim.
Identify one variable to test (headline, color, price, feature) and write your hypothesis: 'Version B will increase signup rate from 3% to 4%'.
Split your traffic or audience 50/50, serve version A to one group and version B to the other; ensure you can measure the outcome.
Collect data for 1-4 weeks (depending on traffic) until your result is statistically significant (p < 0.05); don't stop early to celebrate a trend.
Calculate the effect size (how much better?), not just whether there's a difference; small differences aren't always worth keeping.
If price matters most, test customers' willingness to trade features for lower price using a simple conjoint exercise (show combinations, ask preference).
List research databases, report subscriptions, and free resources relevant to your industry (IBISWorld, Gartner, trade associations, Google Trends).
Find one major report on your market (size, growth, trends, drivers, forecast) and document the key facts and assumptions.
If available, find a second industry report on the same market; note where they agree and where they differ, and why.
From the reports, note: market size, growth rate, key segments, competitor activity, regulatory trends, and customer priorities.
Do desk research on your own category: read articles, analyst reports, earnings calls, customer reviews, and compile a competitor matrix.
List your top 5 competitors and subscribe to their announcements (job postings, press releases, funding news, product launches, pricing changes).
Visit a competitor's site and document: their positioning (who do they target?), messaging (what problem do they emphasize?), features (what's their focus?), pricing (how do they price?).
Create a positioning map: plot your competitors and yourself on two dimensions (price vs. simplicity, speed vs. features, etc.) and find white space.
Look up a competitor's recent news, social media, job postings, and product updates; what does this suggest they're building or prioritizing?
Based on competitor research, identify one gap in the market (feature they don't offer, segment they ignore, price point they don't cover).
Name 10 free or cheap sources of relevant data: government statistics, academic research, nonprofit reports, community discussions, business registries, news archives.
Find free market-size estimates (US Census Bureau, Bureau of Labor Statistics, trade association reports, Google Trends) for your category.
If competitors are public, read their 10-K and earnings calls to learn: revenue, growth, strategy, risk factors, customer concentration.
Collect free feedback: Glassdoor reviews of competitors, Twitter discussions of your industry, Reddit communities, Capterra/G2 reviews, customer interviews.
Compile free data into one place (spreadsheet or wiki): market size, growth, customers, competitors, pricing, trends; refresh quarterly.
Conduct 15-20 interviews with people who fit your target, asking: their job, goals, current solution, pain points, and how they decide.
From interviews, create 2-3 personas with: a name, job title, goals, pain points, how they currently solve it, and why they'd consider switching.
Share your persona with people in the company (sales, support, product); do they recognize this person? Does your persona match their experience?
For three personas, describe differences in: priorities, budget, risk tolerance, and how you'd position to each differently.
Once you're live, track: which customer segments convert best, retain best, and spend most? Update personas based on real behavior.
Analyze your customer data: heavy users vs. light, frequent purchasers vs. one-time, active community members vs. lurkers; describe each segment.
Ask customers about values and motivations: Are they price-sensitive or quality-first? Risk-averse or early adopters? Social or solitary?
Of your segments, which is most profitable? Most satisfied? Most likely to expand? Most likely to refer? Pick your priority segment.
For two segments with different motivations, write different marketing messages emphasizing what matters most to each.
Run an experiment: target your highest-value segment with tailored messaging and compare conversion to untargeted messaging.
Ask 10-15 customers: What task or outcome matters most to you? What gets in the way? What would ideal success look like?

steps.t: List the jobs they want done
steps.d: Synthesize interviews into 3-5 jobs-to-be-done (e.g., 'Help me organize my team' or 'Prove ROI to my boss'), ranked by importance.
For each job, list what customers do today (workarounds, existing tools, manual process) even if none of it's a direct competitor.
For your product, explain what job you're best at and why you're better than the alternatives (including doing nothing).
Create marketing copy focused on the job (not features): 'Make your remote team feel connected' beats 'Real-time collaboration features'.
Collect all your research data (interviews notes, survey results, competitive analysis, industry trends) in one place: shared document, wiki, or research tool.
Create themes or categories from your research: customer needs, objections, decision factors, competitive advantages, market trends.
Summarize key findings in one table: What we learned, why it matters, confidence level (high/medium/low), and what we should do.
What questions are still unanswered? Where do you have medium or low confidence? Plan research to fill the biggest gaps.
Write a clear summary (2-3 pages) of: customer needs, personas, market size, competitive landscape, key assumptions, and recommended next steps.
For your research, identify the headline finding, supporting evidence, and recommended action; put them in narrative order (not data order).
Will you present a written report, slides, video, interactive dashboard, or memo? Match format to audience (executives prefer brevity, stakeholders want detail).
Research reports are most interesting when they challenge assumptions; lead with findings that surprised you or differ from conventional wisdom.
Support each claim with data: quotes from customers, survey percentages, competitive examples; show your work so readers trust your interpretation.
Don't just present findings; end with: 'Based on this, we should...' with 2-3 specific next steps (product, positioning, target segment).
For one specific stakeholder, write the decision they are making and the one key number or outcome that would change their choice.
In the first 30 seconds, state your main finding and why it matters; bury data in appendix for those who want it.
Structure your presentation: what we asked, what we found, what it means, what we recommend; make it a story, not a data dump.
Anticipate objections and address them: How did you recruit? How large was your sample? What could explain this finding alternatively?
End not with data but with decisions: 'This means we should target X segment' or 'We need to cut this feature'; get agreement before you leave.
